title: From Amul to Wow! Momo, Indian Food Brands Are Going Global
excerpt: Amul milk is in 38 US states, Parle exports to 150-plus countries and LT Foods just bought a US brand: India's food companies are manufacturing, partnering and acquiring their way into mainstream overseas supermarkets.
body:
• Indian food brands are expanding abroad at a new scale: Amul's fresh milk is now sold in 38 of 50 US states, Parle exports to more than 150 countries, and Wow! Momo sells packaged food in 14 countries, ET BrandEquity reports.
  • The playbook has changed from shipping packets to diaspora stores: brands are manufacturing locally with foreign partners, tying up with mainstream supermarket chains, and buying overseas brands outright.
  • LT Foods last week agreed to buy US packaged-foods company MK Foods Holdings, owner of the Maya Kaimal brand, for $5.8 million through its US subsidiary.
  • For diaspora shoppers: the push means fuller-fat milk, fresh curd and restaurant-style Indian products are reaching mainstream US, European and Gulf shelves, not just ethnic grocery stores.

Indian food brands are no longer content with a shelf in the ethnic aisle. In a detailed survey of the sector, ET BrandEquity reports that the country's biggest food names are expanding overseas with local manufacturing, mainstream retail partnerships and acquisitions — and, increasingly, selling to local customers abroad, not only to the diaspora.

Amul takes the cooperative model abroad

The most striking expansion is Amul's. The dairy cooperative launched its Amul Gold fresh milk, with 6% fat, in the United States about two years ago, in a market used to milk at 2-3% fat. Sales are doubling year on year, according to the report. Rather than exporting from India, Amul has tied up with cooperatives to manufacture locally: the century-old Michigan Milk Producers Association in the US and COVAP in Spain produce Amul milk for North America and Europe. Amul products are now sold in 38 of 50 American states, as well as Spain, Portugal, Germany, the Netherlands and France, and the brand is present in Japan, with French fries selling now and cheese to follow. In Canada, Amul's single largest product is a vegetarian burger patty.

"You have to find a way to scale the cooperative model globally, as we have with MMPA in the US and COVAP in Spain."

— Jayen Mehta, Managing Director, Amul

Mehta told the publication that Amul almost never needs to localise tastes overseas beyond regulatory compliance: "Indians abroad want the same dal makhani as they have in a restaurant in Delhi."

Restaurants, biscuits and a $10 billion snack bet

Wow! Momo Foods began selling its packaged momos, noodles and kulfis in 14 countries a year ago, including Saudi Arabia, Russia, Singapore, New Zealand, the UK and Germany, through partners such as LuLu Group, Amazon and Carrefour in the Middle East and Mustafa Centre in Singapore. From January, it starts its restaurant business in Sri Lanka with three outlets in Colombo and 20 planned over the first two years, followed by Dubai, Abu Dhabi and Sharjah in the UAE, co-founder Sagar Daryani said.

Parle exports biscuits to more than 150 countries and manufactures in 10 of them, including Mexico and Bahrain; overseas markets contribute 10% of its total turnover. Haldiram's, meanwhile, drew investment last year from Temasek, International Holding Company, Alpha Wave Global and L Catterton at a valuation of over $10 billion for Haldiram Snacks Food, with the investors betting on expansion in large diaspora markets such as the US and the Middle East.

Buying brands, not just shelf space

The newest route is acquisition. LT Foods, the owner of the Daawat and Royal rice brands, announced last week that its US subsidiary, LT Foods Americas, will acquire 100% of MK Foods Holdings, the parent of Maya Kaimal Foods, for an enterprise value of $5.8 million on a cash-free, debt-free basis. Maya Kaimal sells premium Indian-inspired shelf-stable sauces, ready-to-eat curries and rice products in the US and reported revenue of $17.9 million for the 12 months ended September 30, 2026, according to the company's exchange filing. The deal is expected to close within three months.

Why it is working now

Parle's chief marketing officer, Mayank Shah, attributed the surge to more than diaspora demand: "Growing Indian diaspora, students, and tourism are all reasons, but the recent push has been local populations taking to Indian foods. It's the Indianness of taste and formats that's working." The report describes a shift from heat-and-eat and ready-to-cook products toward freshly packaged foods and beverages, with brands investing in local production and supermarket tie-ups to hold shelf space in mainstream stores.

For Indian shoppers abroad, the practical effect is already visible: the brands and formats they grew up with — full-fat milk, fresh paneer and curd, namkeens, biscuits and ready curries — are increasingly stocked where they do their regular weekly shopping, in the US, Canada, the Gulf, Europe and Australia, rather than requiring a separate trip to a specialty store.
